powertable.text: Power Table brings planning into Microsoft Fabric. I designed the Gantt and resource experiences end to end, and contributed to Cross-tab configuration. This portfolio presents selected workflows from that work.
So, what was the challenge? Connect tasks, time, and capacity.
First, map the tasks. This screen shows Start Date, End Date or Duration, and Task I D beside the planning view. Source fields have explicit roles before the planner interprets the timeline.
Next, configure Gantt beside the plan. Timeline, milestone, dependency, color, and label settings have separate jobs, so a planner can find the relevant control without losing context.
Then, review resources in their own planning context. View settings and conditional rules remain separate, so assignment data, layout, and rule meaning do not become one mixed-up task.

Here is the wider product for context. This official product image shows the workspace around the selected features. Open the original to inspect the report; the feature stories explain the design decisions in detail.

And to wrap up. My work covered end-to-end Gantt and resource experience design, plus Cross-tab configuration. These selected cases show the decisions behind that work. Baseline planning and resource earned-value remain labelled explorations.

mapping.text: Let's look at Column Mapping. Before a planner can use the timeline, the product needs to know what each column actually means. Is it a task, a time entry, a resource, or a cost? My work covered the Gantt and resource mapping experience end to end.
So, what was the challenge? Tasks, time entries, resources, and costs need distinct meanings.
First, identify task fields and their dates. Mapping gives each source column a planning role. A useful timeline depends on those meanings, not just familiar column names.
Next, connect time entries using Task I D and logged hours. The shared identifier explains which task the effort belongs to, making the relationship visible rather than assumed.

Then, map resources. This screen shows the resource table, the identifier in the current table, the matching resource identifier, and the display column. The relationship is explicit before that data is used elsewhere.
Now, let's look at the actual design screen. You can open the original for a closer look. It shows a design state, not a recording of the product or, by itself, proof that every interaction shipped.

And to wrap up. There are five supplied design states here. My work went through user experience and interface design, developer handoff, and implementation review. These screens explain the mapping decisions. They don't, on their own, establish runtime behaviour or a measured customer improvement.

baselines.text: Let me take you through Baselines. Say the current schedule has changed, and you want to compare it with a saved reference. That's the idea behind this work. My part was the Gantt comparison experience, and this is still an exploration, not a confirmed release.
So, what was the challenge? A useful comparison needs a clear reference.
First, select the current plan and a saved reference. This exploration limits comparison to two selections in total, keeping the timeline readable instead of stacking many references.
Next, read the current plan alongside the visually distinct reference. Shared timeline context makes the difference explainable against a visible plan, rather than memory.
Then, manage saved baselines in a separate surface. Administration should not interrupt comparison. These exploration screens do not establish a baseline creation flow.
Now, let's look at the actual design screen. You can open the original for a closer look. It shows a design state, not a recording of the product or, by itself, proof that every interaction shipped.

And to wrap up. This is still an exploration. The supplied states cover comparison selection, the timeline, and baseline-management crops. They don't show a baseline-creation flow, or establish that a comparison feature was released. I'm keeping that distinction clear rather than presenting a design exploration as a shipped outcome.

backlog.text: Let's talk about the Backlog. A task may not have dates yet, but it still needs a place beside the plan. I designed the Gantt backlog experience end to end, including how it starts empty and how pending changes are shown.
So, what was the challenge? An empty backlog still needs a useful next step.
First, use the empty backlog as a starting point for adding work. An explained next action is more useful than a blank panel, especially when a task does not have dates yet.
Next, review task rows and their actions beside the schedule. The backlog remains connected to the planning context instead of becoming a separate, unexplained list.
Then, check the pending indicator. An edit that has not been persisted must look different from saved work. The supplied design screens do not verify database persistence.
Now, let's look at the actual design screen. You can open the original for a closer look. It shows a design state, not a recording of the product or, by itself, proof that every interaction shipped.

And to wrap up. The two supplied states explain the backlog design and its pending changes. They don't verify that those changes were saved to a database. So, this is design evidence, not a claim about persistence or a measured improvement.

ganttPanel.text: Here's the Gantt Side Panel. The aim is quite simple: let planners change timeline settings without taking them away from the plan. I worked on this configuration experience end to end.
So, what was the challenge? Configuration should not obscure the planning context.
First, set working time in the Timeline tab. The screen groups the work week, daily capacity, and holiday exceptions before color and pattern. Calendar choices have a dedicated starting point.
Next, open Dependency. Connector color, line type, and stroke sit together, with the scheduling options below. Task relationships need different controls from a working calendar.
Then, open Label. Choose data-label visibility, font size, and text color in one place. These are three selected configuration screens, not footage of live updates.
Now, let's look at the actual design screen. You can open the original for a closer look. It shows a design state, not a recording of the product or, by itself, proof that every interaction shipped.

And to wrap up. There are five configuration tab states in the supplied designs. They explain the structure of the panel, but they're not a recording of someone using the product. I'm not treating those static states as proof of every interaction or a measured outcome.

formatting.text: Let's look at Conditional Formatting for the resource Gantt. A rule has a condition, a set of targets, and a visual style. My work covered that rule-editing experience end to end. The important part was not to mix up what a rule means with how it looks.
So, what was the challenge? People need to distinguish a condition from its appearance.
First, define the condition. Schedule hours greater than zero identifies scheduled work. It does not establish overload, so the rule must not imply a capacity problem.
Next, choose the targets. What matches the condition and which parts of the view are affected are separate decisions. Neither should be hidden inside the color choice.
Then, choose the appearance. Condition, scope, and style together explain the visual signal. The supplied evidence stops at rule editing, not an applied timeline result.
Now, let's look at the actual design screen. You can open the original for a closer look. It shows a design state, not a recording of the product or, by itself, proof that every interaction shipped.

And to wrap up. The evidence shows one rule-editing state. It doesn't show a result after pressing Apply, so I'm not claiming that result or an improvement in capacity planning. What you can inspect here is the design of the rule editor.

resourcePanel.text: Let me take you through the Resource Side Panel. This is about adjusting a resource planning view without losing its context. I designed the resource Gantt configuration experience end to end.
So, what was the challenge? Capacity, task styling, and labels need clear boundaries.
First, set working time in the resource Timeline tab. Work week, daily capacity, and holiday exceptions share one group. These are calendar settings, not proof of capacity accuracy.
Next, open Data Color. This screen shows fill and summary-bar color choices. They style the resource view directly; data-driven conditions belong to the separate conditional-formatting editor.
Then, open Label. Data labels and adaptive labels have their own visibility, font size, and text-color settings. Readability stays separate from resource color choices.
Now, let's look at the actual design screen. You can open the original for a closer look. It shows a design state, not a recording of the product or, by itself, proof that every interaction shipped.

And to wrap up. The supplied evidence covers four configuration states. The conditional-formatting rule editor is a separate feature, with its own evidence. These screens explain the design; they don't establish every runtime interaction or a measured improvement.

crosstab.text: Cross-tab uses rows, columns, and measures to organise the same data from different perspectives. My contribution covered layout and data configuration. This story explains that relationship with a labelled conceptual illustration.
So, what was the challenge? Rows and columns organize the same measures.
First, choose a row dimension. It determines one part of the reading structure, helping an analyst understand why the same dataset can be organized in different ways.
Next, choose a column dimension. Columns add a second perspective on the data. Rows and columns are complementary layout choices, not interchangeable labels.
Then, relate the measure to those dimensions. Measures supply the values within the structure. This is a contribution-level explanation, not a fabricated final interface or measured outcome.

Now, a quick note about what you're seeing. There's no dedicated design screen supplied for this case. This illustration explains my contribution; it's not a final interface or a recording of the product.

And to wrap up. This is contribution-level work. There are no dedicated design screens or measured outcomes supplied for this case. So, I'm explaining the configuration concept and my part in it, without claiming a final interface or whole-product ownership.

analyticsSuite.text: I worked on Analytics Plus user experience and interface design end to end in Power B I. This portfolio presents selected features from that broader work: Chart Wizard, reusable metric templates, Storyboard, Gantt, annotations, and presentation.
So, what was the challenge? Connect discovery, authoring, and presentation.
First, discover a visual through a known chart or an analytical question. Chart Wizard brings these starting points into shared configuration, rather than separate setup systems.

Next, shape a report in Storyboard. This authoring screen combines metric cards, charts, and a table. It is one selected example of my end-to-end Analytics Plus work; the individual feature stories show the other tasks.

Then, explain the insight near the report through annotation and presentation. The audience needs context, not only a chart. Chart Wizard and reusable metric-template delivery are confirmed; other feature states keep their own scope.

Here is the wider product for context. This official product image shows the workspace around the selected features. Open the original to inspect the report; the feature stories explain the design decisions in detail.

And to wrap up. These are selected examples from my end-to-end Analytics Plus work, from workflows and interface design through developer handoff and implementation review. Chart Wizard and reusable metric templates shipped. Each feature keeps its original evidence.

wizard.text: Let me quickly walk you through Chart Wizard. Sometimes you already know the chart you want. Other times, you just know the question you need to answer. I worked on the full Chart Wizard flow, from user experience and interface design through handoff and implementation review.
So, what was the challenge? People start with either a known chart or an analytical question.
First, discover a chart. Browse Chart families when you know the visual, or start with Function when you know the analytical question. Both routes lead toward the same configuration workflow.
Next, customize styling and visibility. Keeping appearance choices together helps the author focus on presentation without facing every analytical control at once.

Then, use Advanced for analytical settings and sorting. Both discovery routes share this configuration, while Favorites stay in discovery. Different starting needs do not require duplicate settings systems.
Now, let's look at the actual design screen. You can open the original for a closer look. It shows a design state, not a recording of the product or, by itself, proof that every interaction shipped.

And to wrap up. Chart Wizard shipped. My work covered the flow end to end, including handoff, walkthroughs, and implementation checks. The screens show the design decisions behind that delivery. They don't, by themselves, prove a measured usability improvement or customer outcome.

storyboard.text: Let's look at Storyboard. Not every report starts the same way. You might want a template, a custom layout, or just a blank canvas. I worked on the feature experience, developer handoff, and implementation review.
So, what was the challenge? Authors may need a template, custom layout, or blank report.
First, choose a template, custom layout, or blank report. The starting route reflects how much structure the author needs, instead of forcing everyone into one setup.
Next, establish the layout for that route. Understanding the structure before arranging content connects report creation with composition.
Then, continue into the authoring canvas. The chosen starting structure stays connected to editing. Supplied screens explain the journey but do not verify every interaction.
Now, let's look at the actual design screen. You can open the original for a closer look. It shows a design state, not a recording of the product or, by itself, proof that every interaction shipped.

And to wrap up. The six supplied screens cover report authoring and template states. Presentation is a separate contribution. These are design and product screens, not a recording of the complete journey or proof that every state was released.

gantt.text: Here's the Gantt work inside Analytics Plus for Power B I. Before task data becomes a useful timeline, its fields need clear meanings. I worked on the feature experience, handoff, and implementation review. This is separate from the Power Table work in Microsoft Fabric.
So, what was the challenge? Source columns must acquire task and date meanings.
First, choose Gantt within Analytics Plus for Power B I. The timeline begins in the chart-selection workflow, not the separate Power Table product in Microsoft Fabric.
Next, assign task, start-date, and end-date fields. Clear column roles explain what the schedule will represent before the author interprets the timeline.
Then, read the timeline in relation to the mapped fields. The design connects source data with schedule context. These states do not establish measured scheduling accuracy.
Now, let's look at the actual design screen. You can open the original for a closer look. It shows a design state, not a recording of the product or, by itself, proof that every interaction shipped.

And to wrap up. This case covers the Analytics Plus Gantt feature in Power B I, not the Power Table Gantt product in Fabric. The screens explain its design states. They don't, on their own, establish every interaction, a release outcome, or a measured improvement.

presentation.text: Let's talk about annotations and presentation. A chart can show an observation, but people also need the explanation and a clear point of focus. I worked on this feature's experience, handoff, and implementation review.
So, what was the challenge? Connect an observation, its explanation, and the audience’s focus.
First, mark the relevant chart observation. An annotation connects the explanation to a specific point, so the audience knows which part of the report is being discussed.
Next, explain the meaning through a comment and its formatting. Keeping the explanation beside the observation helps the chart communicate a point rather than expecting the data to explain itself.
Then, guide attention in the presentation context. Observation, explanation, and audience focus stay connected. The screens do not establish improved audience understanding in actual use.
Now, let's look at the actual design screen. You can open the original for a closer look. It shows a design state, not a recording of the product or, by itself, proof that every interaction shipped.

And to wrap up. There are nine supplied design screens here. They show annotation and presentation states, but they're not proof of every interaction or release. So, I'm keeping the interface evidence separate from claims about what happened in use.

kpi.text: Let me take you through K P I Presets. Instead of starting every metric card from scratch, authors can use a reusable pattern. My work focused on designing and delivering those reusable K P I templates.
So, what was the challenge? Authors need reusable starting points for cards and comparisons.
First, choose a simple metric pattern or a variance arrangement. Different starting structures serve different reading tasks, so the author does not have to begin every card from scratch.
Next, compare the Variance presets. This screen shows alternate arrangements for a metric and its comparisons beside the report canvas. It is preset selection, not a separate card-authoring screen.

Then, inspect the original pattern sheet. It compares reusable metric-card arrangements side by side. This is design-library evidence, not a working template-management screen. The reusable templates shipped.
Now, let's look at the actual design screen. You can open the original for a closer look. It shows a design state, not a recording of the product or, by itself, proof that every interaction shipped.

And to wrap up. The reusable K P I templates shipped. Other authoring and library screens remain design evidence, not an automatic claim that every state was released. That's the scope of the contribution shown here.

spatial.text: This is Analytics Plus, explored beyond the screen. Three concept frames carry a familiar application workflow into a spatial setting. They are not a shipped Vision Pro product or validated interaction.

The design question is how to keep entry and report viewing recognizable in a spatial environment. Familiar structure is an orientation hypothesis, not proof of comfort, readability, or accessibility.
First, launch from the proposed app launcher in the room-like environment. This frame introduces a recognizable starting point without claiming tested gaze, gesture, or physical interaction behavior.

Next, enter Analytics Plus in a floating window. Keeping the familiar application identity connects the entry experience to the spatial proposal. Whether that continuity helps users still needs validation.

Then, view the report frame with charts and a table. The familiar destination carries into the proposal, but readable text, comfortable placement, accessibility, and interaction are not established by an image.
The evidence is three authored concept frames: launch, entry, and report. You can inspect the original sequence. These are visual proposals, not footage or working spatial interactions.
This remains a concept exploration. Gaze, gestures, comfort, accessibility, and spatial controls need real testing. There is no Vision Pro release or measured user benefit claimed here.

bikecare.text: BikeCare is an Indian two-wheeler UX and UI concept. Motorcycles, scooters, mopeds and electric vehicles have separate care needs. Riders and local workshop teams connect approval, records, reminders and recovery. This is a design prototype, not a production app.

The starting observation is local servicing, forgotten care and missing resale records. GarageMate, Hero and Royal Enfield already document relevant features. Public-source desk research guides this design; interviews and usability results are not invented.

First, approve the service. The advisor records the complaint, intake and itemised estimate. The rider approves this version before mechanic work. Additional parts require fresh approval. Brand-style job cards do not imply manufacturer integration.

Next, carry care forward. Work, billing and rider review stay separate. Optional feedback follows confirmation; only requested follow-up creates a complaint. Confirmed history supports supplied reminders and private resale. Unknown intervals stay blank.

Then, connect parts and rides. Supplier review is not proof of every part genuine. Check fit and manufacturer evidence. Public, club and company motorcycle rides need organiser review. Exact meetup details remain private; joining is not a safety guarantee.

Explore vehicle and EV setup, access recovery, workshop handovers, care, shopping, motorcycle rides and support. Switch the custom light and dark themes. The case names its scenario coverage and limits. Every account, transaction and trip is fictional.

The business case is useful care beyond one visit: clearer workshop handovers, maintenance cues, resale records, relevant parts and motorcycle communities. Adoption, repeat purchases and resale gains are hypotheses. No business or primary-research results are claimed.
